“Gödel proved that nothing is certain and truth is relative.” Wrong. The theorem is itself the result of a rigorous proof. A statement that cannot be proved in system A can often be proved in a stronger system B.
“Every system is incomplete.” Wrong. Presburger arithmetic (addition only) and Tarski’s theory of Euclidean geometry are both complete, because they do not meet the conditions.

blocks.h: So “truth is bigger than proof” must be said with care. It does not mean that some truths can never be proved under any circumstances. It means that no single fixed axiom system can capture all the truths of arithmetic. The Swedish mathematician Torkel Franzén wrote an entire book devoted to clearing up the uses and abuses of this theorem.

Mathematics really does contain such examples. Goodstein’s theorem (proved in 1944) cannot be proved in Peano arithmetic (Kirby & Paris, 1982). The continuum hypothesis is independent of the standard axioms of set theory (Cohen, 1963–64). Gentzen did prove the consistency of Peano arithmetic in 1936, but he used a stronger principle from outside the system.
Gödel himself

He was baptized as a Lutheran but belonged to no church. He described his own belief as theism, following Leibniz rather than Spinoza, and he believed in an afterlife. His wife said he often read the Bible in bed on Sunday mornings. He also wrote that most religions are bad, but religion itself is not. This is not the same as evangelical faith, and we should not say more on his behalf than he said.

He also left behind a manuscript of an “ontological proof,” arguing in modal logic that God exists. The earliest version dates to around 1941, and he gave it to Dana Scott in 1970. He never published it, reportedly for fear that people would think he really believed in God. Later, computers verified that the reasoning is valid, but the verifiers also said that whether the premises hold remains a human responsibility; Sobel went further and pointed out that these axioms lead to a “modal collapse,” in which everything that is true becomes necessarily true. Valid logic does not mean a true conclusion.
Let us separate mathematical theorem, scholarly debate and faith reflection.
The first and second incompleteness theorems hold for consistent, axiomatizable formal systems that contain basic arithmetic. They are rigorously proved mathematical theorems.
The theorems do not apply to every system: Presburger arithmetic and Tarski’s theory of Euclidean geometry are complete.

Lucas (1961) and Penrose (1989, 1994) argued that the theorems show the human mind is not a machine. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy notes that the field generally regards these arguments as failing, because people cannot always see whether a system is consistent.

Gödel regarded himself as a theist and believed in an afterlife; the biographical material comes from his unsent questionnaire, his wife’s accounts and the like, and is not a complete confession of faith.

The theorems can neither prove nor disprove God. What they can offer is a humbling analogy: if even arithmetic cannot be exhausted by a single fixed axiom system, then human grasp of truth also has limits. This is philosophical and theological reflection, not a consequence of the theorem.
The viewpoints room
What do the theorems mean for the “human mind” and for “reason”?

items.h: Lucas and Penrose argued that people can see that the Gödel sentence is true while a machine system cannot, so the mind is not an algorithm. Most logicians do not accept this, holding that we know it only on the assumption that the system is consistent.

Gödel himself did not become pessimistic because of this. He believed reason could keep making progress and that many problems would eventually be solved. Incompleteness does not mean reason is useless, only that it cannot be sealed inside one fixed set of rules.
Christians can take it as a reminder that reason has limits, and speak of trust beyond those limits. But the theorem must not be presented as proof of faith. Trust itself also needs reasons.

blocks.h: Having limits does not mean being useless
The Bible never tells anyone to switch off their mind. Jesus said to love God with all your mind. But Paul also knew that what we understand now is not everything.
For we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when that which is complete has come, then that which is partial will be done away with.
Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.
Truth is a person
Pilate asked Jesus, “What is truth?” and walked out without waiting for an answer. Yet only hours earlier Jesus had said something to His disciples that no axiom system could hold.
Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.

This does not mean that faith needs no evidence. The disciples saw the risen Jesus with their own eyes, and they were ready to give people their reasons. But knowing a person is different from proving a theorem. You can use evidence to see that your spouse is trustworthy, and in the end you still have to entrust yourself. God did not put salvation inside a proof that only geniuses can read. He let His beloved Son be nailed to a cross, and raised Him up, so that everyone could come.
because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.

Take something you are completely sure of but cannot fully explain, such as the fact that you love a certain person. Write it down. Then write down one thing you want to admit to God: “I do not know.” Then say to Him: But I know that You know me.
Meditate: do I often insist on fitting God into my logic before I will trust Him? Or do I use “faith” as an excuse because I am too lazy to think?

Pray: God of wisdom, thank You for giving me a mind that can think, and thank You for letting me run into its limits. Forgive my pride, and forgive my laziness. Thank You, Lord Jesus, that You are the truth, that You died for me and rose again. Help me to love You with all my mind, and to trust You with all my heart. In Jesus’ name, amen.
321 Life Application

items: Humility overcomes pride: if even arithmetic cannot be exhausted by one set of rules, I can practice saying, “I am not sure about this.”
The Bible is my standard: be accurate when citing scholars and theorems. Overstating things for the sake of faith damages our witness.
Letting God be God and people be people: I do not have to prove everything, and I do not have to stop thinking. I hand the outcome to Him.

blocks.h: This week: look up one claim you often repeat, either “science proves faith” or “science refutes faith,” find the original source, and see what it actually said.
Pass it on: Is the thing you are most sure of in life something you can prove?
Quiz

quiz.q: What does the first incompleteness theorem apply to?
o: All mathematical systems and all knowledge
Formal systems that are consistent, axiomatizable and contain enough arithmetic
quiz.e: Systems that do not meet the conditions, such as addition-only Presburger arithmetic, are actually complete.

quiz.q: Which of the following statements is correct?
o: Gödel proved that truth is relative
The theorems can neither prove God nor imply that truth is relative
quiz.e: These are the two most common abuses. The theorems are about the limits of formal systems.

quiz.q: What does it mean that a computer “verified” Gödel’s ontological proof?
o: The reasoning is formally valid, but whether the premises hold still has to be judged by people
Science has proved that God exists
Gödel’s premises were confirmed to be true
quiz.e: The verifiers themselves said that critical discussion of the concepts and axioms remains a human responsibility.

questions.q: Why can math worked out on paper describe the whole universe so precisely?
Can finite people know an infinite God?
Could all of this just be coincidence?
